problem: End-to-end RL visual navigation policies overfit to training environments, and naively reusing pretrained visual representations (e.g. concatenating Taskonomy features, feature-level fusion) gives only marginal gains and is brittle to noise or failure of a representation.
motivation: Navigation needs different perception skills in different situations (semantics for finding objects, depth/3D for avoiding obstacles). Feature-level fusion is biased toward a few dominant representations and under-trains the others, so it overfits. A fusion scheme that is situational and redundancy-aware should generalize to unseen homes.
key_idea: Fuse 25 Taskonomy visual representations at the action level: each representation predicts its own action candidate, a state-dependent softmax gate combines them, and a Taskonomy task-affinity bilinear regularizer on the gate weights penalizes co-selecting redundant representations.
insight: Action-level fusion trains each branch to be a valid policy and acts like an ensemble. Train performance is similar to feature-level fusion but test performance is far better (avg SR 40.3 vs 23.1), and majority voting alone is already competitive (41.1). The affinity regularizer adds a further gain that the generic load-balancing loss does not (44.2 vs 39.8 avg SR, with the biggest gains on table and chair). The learned gates are interpretable: 3D representations dominate in narrow corridors and semantic ones in cluttered areas. The action-level scheme also degrades more gracefully when representations are dropped or zeroed.
method: Representation bank: 25 pretrained Taskonomy encoders map each RGB image to a 16x16x8 representation, covering 2D, 3D and semantic tasks.
Action-level fusion: an independent action-prediction module per representation outputs an action candidate, and the final action is sum_i g_i * pi'_i(r_i).
Situational-fusion network: takes the RGB observation and outputs n logits, and a softmax gives state-dependent fusion weights g_t.
Inter-task affinity regularization: loss L_g = g^T F g, where F_ij is the Taskonomy pairwise affinity. It penalizes putting large weight on high-affinity, redundant pairs.
Supervision: optimal actions come from shortest paths on a precomputed octagonal-grid graph, with Adam, 16K iterations and batch size 256.
Baselines and ablations: ResNet-50 (ImageNet), Concat, feature-level fusion, LBL loss, majority voting and Top-k voting.

setting.backbone: Frozen pretrained Taskonomy encoders (25 tasks) + trained per-representation action heads and fusion network; ResNet-50 baseline
setting.training_data: Supervised shortest-path optimal actions in about 28 Gibson/Matterport3D environments per task (62 environments total); Taskonomy encoders pretrained on the Taskonomy dataset
setting.observation: 8 RGB images in octagonal directions from a 360-degree camera
setting.action_space: discrete high-level: 8 grid step directions + stop on an octagonal grid
setting.privileged: GT object annotations and grid graph used for training supervision only; none at test

numbers_note: Custom benchmark, not a standard one. Baseline and ablation numbers appear in Table 1 (ResNet avg 20.9, Concat 25.6, feature-level Both 31.2, Maj. 41.1). Robustness and per-branch results are only in figures.
results: Action-level fusion with task-affinity regularization reaches 44.2 avg SR in unseen environments, about 2x the ImageNet ResNet-50 baseline (20.9) and better than Concat (25.6), the best feature-level fusion (31.2) and majority voting (41.1). It is also more robust when representations are dropped or zeroed.
limitations: Evaluated only on a simulated high-level octagonal-grid task with 4 object categories; no real-robot tests or standard benchmarks.

Requires running all 25 Taskonomy encoders per step (computationally heavy) and depends on Taskonomy affinities. The gain of T.Aff over plain action-level fusion is modest (about 3 points avg SR), and the 'Both' variant is slightly lower on average.
